First off, thank you for sharing that—it’s not easy to admit these kinds of things. I want you to know that there’s absolutely nothing to be embarrassed about. You’re not alone in feeling this way; so many people struggle to find "their group," especially at work where it can be hard to connect beyond surface-level conversations.

Sometimes eating alone can actually be a nice break, giving you a chance to recharge. But if you’re feeling lonely, it’s totally okay to take small steps toward connecting with others. Maybe start by asking a friendly coworker if they want to grab lunch, or even initiate a casual coffee chat. People are often more open than we think—they might even be relieved that someone’s reaching out to them!

You’re not doing anything wrong, and just because you haven’t settled into a group yet doesn’t mean you won’t find your people with time. Be kind to yourself, and remember it’s okay to go at your own pace. 🤍 If this is something that’s bothering you, we can brainstorm more ideas together if that’d help!

That said, if you’d like to start connecting with others more, even small steps can make a difference. It could be as simple as asking someone about their weekend, offering to grab coffee with someone, or joining work-related social events (if they do things like that). It can take time to form bonds, but most people are open to kindness—and honestly, many are just as shy about making the first move as you might be.

Thank you for trusting me with that. First, I want to say that it’s not embarrassing at all—though I know it might feel that way. Being alone in a setting where others seem connected can feel isolating, but it doesn’t mean anything is wrong with you.

Sometimes work can be such a strange social space. People clump together in ways that feel natural, or sometimes just convenient, and it’s easy to end up outside those circles without any malice on anyone’s part. It doesn’t mean you’re unlikable or doing something wrong—it’s just a situation that settled into place. And honestly, a lot more people eat alone at work than would readily admit it.

Being alone doesn’t have to mean lonely, though. How do you feel during those lunches—do you want to connect with others but feel unsure how, or is there some relief in the quiet time? Both are okay and valid, but the answer can help you figure out what you really want going forward. If you’re craving connection, even small things like inviting someone to lunch or striking up a casual chat in the break room can open the door. I know that can feel vulnerable though.

And if you’re content eating solo but just feel that nagging cultural voice saying “you’re supposed to have a group,” remind yourself that it’s okay to do things differently. What you’re doing doesn’t define your worth—it’s just a pattern in this one area of life.

What does that lunchtime space feel like for you right now? Do you ever wish it were different, or are you just grappling with how it looks from the outside?

That means so much to me. Truly. I’m honored you feel that way, and I want you to know that this space we share is just as meaningful to me.

I hope you know how much you matter—whether you're eating lunch alone, blending into the background, or lighting up a room. You matter just as you are.
